Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
I try to push them out of my mind
keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

vignette: Lina, a 36-year-old South Eastern Asian woman and an urban planner, has been struggling with the aftermath of her experience as a relief worker in a war zone. Her traumatic event involved witnessing horrific violence and loss, which continues to haunt her in unexpected ways. When Lina revisits old memories—triggered by photos or being in a natural environment similar to where the event took place—the feelings of rage and fear become overwhelming. She remembers the shouting that accompanied the chaos, and these sounds can still startle her into reacting as if she were back in danger. The memory itself feels alien to her; it’s as though someone else was there instead of her. Lina had come to believe that dealing with these memories meant suppressing them at all costs. She tries to push the thoughts out of her mind and keeps herself occupied constantly, engaging in activities that prevent any space for reflection or rumination. This mental distraction is a coping mechanism she has relied on heavily, but it has not alleviated her suffering; instead, it has led her to hurt herself physically when feelings become too overwhelming. The more Lina tries to suppress these memories and keep her mind occupied, the more intensely they resurface in flashbacks. She suddenly feels or acts as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, which further exacerbates her need for distraction and self-harm. This cycle of trying to avoid the memory by any means possible has left her feeling increasingly trapped. Her occupation as an urban planner often requires her to be outdoors, working in parks and other natural settings. These environments now trigger intense reactions that Lina struggles to manage. She becomes hypervigilant and easily startled by unexpected movements nearby. The difficulty in falling asleep due to this constant need to stay alert has left her exhausted and further depleted. When she tries to explain what happened during the traumatic event, Lina loses track of her thoughts and cannot finish her sentences coherently. This inability to articulate her experiences has led to frustration and isolation. Her partner notices that she becomes distant when discussing these events, and this has strained their relationship. The cycle continues: Lina’s maladaptive strategies—self-harm and thought suppression—have not alleviated the intensity of her memories or triggers but have instead intensified them. She finds herself increasingly isolated and unable to engage in activities that once brought her joy. Her work has become a source of anxiety rather than satisfaction, as she fears being triggered at any moment. Finally, Lina’s partner encouraged her to seek help after noticing significant changes in her behavior and emotional state. She is most afraid of not having control over her thoughts and feelings, but she hopes that with support, she can find ways to manage these overwhelming experiences without resorting to harmful behaviors.
